blocks.text: Practice long questions for the whole of Chapter 17 (Group 2 Elements), in the shape of a Board long question: each theory question carries 4 marks (describe, explain, give equations, draw where needed), and the chapter's numericals are solved step by step. Each question has a full model answer.

blocks.prompt: 1 Describe the general characteristics of Group 2 elements: their position, name, occurrence, electronic configuration and some important uses mentioned in the chapter. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Position: Group 2 elements (Be, Mg, Ca, Sr, Ba) are s block elements in Group 2 of the periodic table.

Name: they are called alkaline earth metals due to their metallic nature and occurrence in the earth crust. Their reactivity lies between the highly reactive alkali metals and the less reactive transition metals.

Occurrence: Ca and Mg are among the eight most widely occurring elements in the earth crust.

Electronic configuration: all have two electrons in the outermost s subshell (ns²): Be [He] 2s², Mg [Ne] 3s², Ca [Ar] 4s², Sr [Kr] 5s², Ba [Xe] 6s². Therefore they show similar chemical properties, though properties vary from top to bottom.

Uses: Be makes copper alloys harder for aerospace materials; Mg is an important part of chlorophyll; Mg, Ca, Sr and Ba are essential components of fireworks due to their vibrant flame colours.

book_ref.quote: These elements present a class of metals having reactivity between

blocks.prompt: 2 Using the data of Table 17.1, describe the trends from Be to Ba in metallic radius, ionic radius, ionization energies, electronegativity and standard electrode potential. How are melting point and density different? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
From Table 17.1 (Be → Ba):
• Metallic radius increases: 112, 160, 197, 215, 222 pm.
• Ionic radius of M²⁺ increases: 31, 65, 99, 113, 135.
• First ionization energy decreases: 900, 738, 590, 550, 503; second ionization energy also decreases: 1757, 1451, 1145, 1064, 965.
• Electronegativity decreases: 1.5, 1.2, 1.0, 1.0, 0.9.
• Standard electrode potential becomes more negative from Be to Ba (Ca −2.87, Sr −2.89, Ba −2.91 V), i.e. the metals lose electrons more readily.

Melting point (1287, 650, 842, 777, 727 °C) and density (1.85, 1.74, 1.54, 2.64, 3.51 g/cm³) do not change regularly. These trends are related to the different packing of the metal atoms down the group.

blocks.prompt: 3 Explain the chemical reactivity of Group 2 elements on the basis of their electronic configuration. Why does reactivity increase from Be to Ba? Give the reactivity series. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Electronic configuration: Group 2 elements have two electrons in their outermost subshell (ns²). After losing these two electrons they become stable ions with a +2 charge (M²⁺), so they react quickly with other substances.

Increase in reactivity from Be to Ba, due to:
(i) increase in atomic size (Figure 17.1 shows the atoms getting larger down the group);
(ii) increase in shielding effect by the inner electrons;
(iii) decrease in ionization energy down the group.
These make the removal of the two valence electrons easier, so reactivity increases.

Reactivity series (increasing): Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba
Be is the least reactive and Ba the most reactive element of Group 2.

book_ref.quote: The reactivity of Group 2 elements can be explained based on their electronic configuration

blocks.prompt: 4 Describe the reactions of Group 2 metals with oxygen, giving equations. Explain the nature of the oxides formed. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
General reaction: all Group 2 metals burn in oxygen to form metal oxides, MO:
2M + O₂ → 2MO

Beryllium reacts only at high temperatures (above 600 °C):
2Be(s) + O₂(g) → 2BeO(s)
A thin, strong oxide layer usually protects it, making it less reactive than the other members.

Magnesium burns brightly in air or oxygen to form MgO.
Calcium reacts with oxygen more vigorously, giving a brick red flame (Figure 17.2).

Nature of oxides: Group 2 oxides are generally white solids and basic in nature; their basic character increases down the group. The basic character in water is due to the reaction of the oxide ion with water to produce OH⁻ ions:
O²⁻(s) + H₂O(l) → 2OH⁻(aq)

book_ref.quote: All Group 2 metals burn in oxygen to form metal oxides (MO)

blocks.prompt: 5 Compare the behaviour of beryllium, magnesium and calcium towards cold water and steam, with equations. How does the basic character of the hydroxides change down the group? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
General: except Be, Group 2 metals react with water to give the metal hydroxide M(OH)₂ and hydrogen gas.

Beryllium: does not react with water or steam, even when heated, because of its protective oxide layer.

Magnesium: reacts very slowly with cold water, faster with steam (giving the oxide):
Mg(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Mg(OH)₂ + H₂(g)   (cold water)
Mg(s) + H₂O(g) → MgO(s) + H₂(g)   (steam)

Calcium: reacts with cold water and steam more vigorously than Mg; Ca(OH)₂ is sparingly soluble and forms a white precipitate (Figure 17.3):
Ca(s) + 2H₂O(l) → Ca(OH)₂(aq) + H₂(g)

Basic character: Group 2 hydroxides are less basic than Group 1 hydroxides, but their basic character increases down the group due to increasing solubility.

book_ref.quote: Calcium (Ca) reacts with cold water and steam more vigorously than magnesium

blocks.prompt: 6 Describe the reactions of Group 2 metals with dilute hydrochloric acid and dilute sulphuric acid. Why does the reaction of calcium with sulphuric acid stop early? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
General: Group 2 metals react with dilute acids to give a salt and hydrogen gas; reactivity increases down the group.
M(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)

Beryllium: reacts with dilute acids to form BeCl₂ and H₂, but its protective oxide layer can slow the reaction.

Magnesium: reacts readily with dilute acids:
Mg(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Mg(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → MgSO₄(aq) + H₂(g)

Calcium: reacts vigorously with dilute acids:
Ca(s) + 2HCl(aq) → CaCl₂(aq) + H₂(g)
Ca(s) + H₂SO₄(aq) → CaSO₄(s) + H₂(g)

Reason for early stop: the calcium sulphate formed is sparingly soluble; it coats the metal surface with a protective layer, so the acid can no longer reach the metal and the reaction stops early.

blocks.prompt: 7 Beryllium often behaves differently from the other Group 2 elements. Using the chapter, explain its behaviour towards oxygen, water and dilute acids, and the stability of its carbonate. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Oxygen: Be reacts with oxygen only at high temperatures (above 600 °C) to form BeO; a thin, strong oxide layer usually protects it, so it is less reactive than the other members.

Water: Be does not react with water or steam, even when heated, due to its protective oxide layer (the others give M(OH)₂ and H₂).

Dilute acids: Be reacts to form BeCl₂ and H₂, but its protective oxide layer can slow this reaction.

Carbonate: Be²⁺ is the smallest Group 2 ion with the highest charge density, so it has the greatest polarizing power; it distorts CO₃²⁻ most and BeCO₃ decomposes at the lowest temperature (250 °C, Table 17.3).

Overall, Be is the least reactive element of Group 2 (Be < Mg < Ca < Sr < Ba) because it has the smallest size and highest ionization energy.

book_ref.quote: This is due to its protective oxide layer.

blocks.prompt: 8 Compare Group 1 (alkali metals) with Group 2 (alkaline earth metals) under at least eight headings. Why are both groups more reactive at the bottom? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation: Group 1 metals have only one electron to lose and form +1 ions readily; Group 2 metals lose two electrons, which requires more energy, so they are reactive but generally less so than Group 1 metals in the same period. Both groups show increasing reactivity down the group due to increasing atomic size and decreasing ionization energy.

book_ref.quote: Table 17.2 Comparison of Group 2 elements with Group 1 elements

rows: Less reactive in the same period (higher ionization energies)
Very soft (can be cut with a knife)
Very vigorous, often explosive with water (Na)
Less vigorous with water (Ca with water, Mg with steam)
Hydroxides less soluble (solubility increases down the group), less basic

blocks.prompt: 9 What is thermal decomposition? Explain, in terms of the polarizing power of the cation, why the thermal stability of Group 2 carbonates increases down the group. Support your answer with Table 17.3. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Thermal decomposition: a chemical reaction in which a single compound breaks down into two or more simpler substances when heated; it usually requires energy (endothermic) to break bonds.

Group 2 carbonates decompose to the metal oxide and CO₂:
MgCO₃(s) → MgO(s) + CO₂(g)
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)

Polarizing power: small, highly charged cations such as Be²⁺ have a greater polarizing power. They distort the large carbonate ion (CO₃²⁻) to a larger extent, weakening its bonds and making it easier to decompose with heat. As the M²⁺ ion gets larger down the group, its polarizing power decreases, so the carbonates become more stable and need more heat (compare the polarisation of CO₃²⁻ by Mg²⁺ and by Ba²⁺).

Table 17.3 (decomposition temperature at 1 atm): BeCO₃ 250 °C, MgCO₃ 540 °C, CaCO₃ 900 °C, SrCO₃ 1289 °C, BaCO₃ 1360 °C. BaCO₃ requires the highest temperature.

book_ref.quote: The above discussed trend is due to the size of the M²⁺ ion

blocks.prompt: 10 Describe the thermal decomposition of Group 2 nitrates with a balanced equation for strontium nitrate. State and explain the trend in their thermal stability. How is the decomposition pattern useful to chemists? (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Products: Group 2 nitrates decompose on heating to the metal oxide (MO), brown nitrogen dioxide gas (NO₂) and oxygen gas (O₂). For example:
2Ca(NO₃)₂(s) → 2CaO(s) + 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g)
2Sr(NO₃)₂(s) → 2SrO(s) + 4NO₂(g) + O₂(g)

Trend: as with carbonates, the thermal stability of nitrates increases down Group 2. Be(NO₃)₂ is the least stable and Ba(NO₃)₂ the most stable.

Reason: the smaller M²⁺ ions at the top of the group have greater polarizing power; they distort the nitrate ion (NO₃⁻) more effectively, making its decomposition easier at lower temperatures.

Usefulness: by observing the temperature at which a Group 2 carbonate or nitrate decomposes, chemists can identify unknown compounds and confirm the presence of specific elements. The pattern also shows the relationship between ionic size, charge density and thermal stability.

book_ref.quote: Group 2 nitrates decompose upon heating to form a metal oxide (MO)

blocks.prompt: 11 The solubility of an ionic compound depends on two energy changes. Define enthalpy of hydration, lattice enthalpy and enthalpy of solution, and state the factors that affect the first two. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Enthalpy of hydration (ΔHhyd): the energy released when gaseous ions are surrounded and attracted by water molecules (become hydrated). It is always exothermic (negative).
Factors: stronger attraction between ions and water gives a more negative ΔHhyd. Smaller ions with higher charge density attract water more strongly, giving a more negative (higher) hydration enthalpy. ΔHhyd becomes less negative down a group as the ions get larger.

Lattice enthalpy (ΔHlattice): the energy required to break apart one mole of a solid ionic compound into its gaseous ions. It is always endothermic.
Factors: it depends on the charges and sizes of the ions; stronger forces in the lattice mean a higher lattice enthalpy. When the cation and anion are of comparable size the forces are stronger and the lattice energy is higher; when one ion is large and the other much smaller the forces are weaker and the lattice energy is lower.

Enthalpy of solution (ΔHsoln): the overall energy change when a solid ionic substance is dissolved. A more negative or less positive ΔHsoln generally favours higher solubility.

book_ref.quote: depends on the balance between two main energy changes

blocks.prompt: 12 Down Group 2 both the hydration enthalpy of M²⁺ and the lattice enthalpy decrease. Explain how the size of the anion decides which decrease is larger, and use this to account for the opposite solubility trends of the hydroxides and sulphates, quoting data from Table 17.4. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Down the group the M²⁺ ion gets larger, so both ΔHhyd (of M²⁺) and ΔHlattice decrease. Which decrease is larger depends on the anion.

Hydroxides (small anion, OH⁻): with smaller Group 2 metal ions the lattice energy of the hydroxides is higher, and vice versa. Going down, the decrease in lattice enthalpy is more significant than the decrease in hydration enthalpy, so dissolving becomes easier and solubility increases.
Data (mol/100 g of water, 298 K): Mg(OH)₂ 2 × 10⁻⁵, Ca(OH)₂ 1.5 × 10⁻³, Sr(OH)₂ 3.4 × 10⁻³, Ba(OH)₂ 1.5 × 10⁻² (Mg(OH)₂ sparingly soluble, Ba(OH)₂ quite soluble).

Sulphates (large anion, SO₄²⁻): for a large anion like sulphate, the decrease in hydration enthalpy is more significant than the decrease in lattice enthalpy, so solubility decreases down the group.
Data: MgSO₄ 1.83 × 10⁻¹, CaSO₄ 4.66 × 10⁻³, SrSO₄ 7.11 × 10⁻⁵, BaSO₄ 9.43 × 10⁻⁷ (MgSO₄ soluble, BaSO₄ insoluble).

Thus the two trends are opposite (Figure 17.4).

book_ref.quote: But, for a large anion like sulphate, the decrease in hydration enthalpy is more significant than the decrease in lattice enthalpy

blocks.prompt: 13 Define complex ion and coordination number. Explain the roles of Lewis acid and Lewis base in a complex, and the factors that decide the ability of Group 2 ions to form complexes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Complex ion: an ion in which a central metal is bonded to a number of surrounding electron donating species.

Lewis acid and base: the central metal ion acts as a Lewis acid (electron pair acceptor); molecules or ions with lone pairs, e.g. H₂O, NH₃, Cl⁻, OH⁻, act as Lewis bases.

Coordination number: the number of coordinate bonds formed between the central metal ion and the electron donors; common values are 2, 4 and 6.

Group 2 ions: complex formation is more typical of transition metals (available d-orbitals for bonding); Group 2 ions, especially those at the top of the group, can also form complexes, though the tendency is far less pronounced.
Factors: (i) size: smaller ions have a higher charge density (high charge to size ratio) and attract electron-donating species better; (ii) charge: all Group 2 ions carry +2, which provides electrostatic attraction for electron pair donors.

book_ref.quote: The ability of a Group 2 metal ion to form a complex ion depends on its size and charge

blocks.prompt: 14 Describe the hydrated ions formed by Group 2 metal ions in water and the complex of calcium with EDTA. Give the uses of the EDTA complexes. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Hydrated ions: when Group 2 salts dissolve in water the metal ions become hydrated; these are essentially complex ions in which water molecules act as electron pair donors.
• Be²⁺: smallest ion, high charge density; strongly attracts water and forms [Be(H₂O)₄]²⁺, coordination number 4.
• Mg²⁺: larger; usually forms the hexahydrate [Mg(H₂O)₆]²⁺, coordination number 6.
• Ca²⁺, Sr²⁺, Ba²⁺: also form hydrated ions, mostly with coordination number 6, but the strength of the interaction decreases down the group.

EDTA complex: Group 2 ions, especially the smaller ones, form stable complexes with donors having more than one donatable electron pair; such donors form more than one coordinate bond to the same ion, creating a ring-like structure. Ca²⁺ forms a ring complex with EDTA, a six electron pair donor:
Ca²⁺(aq) + EDTA⁴⁻(aq) → [Ca(EDTA)]²⁻(aq)

Uses: (i) water softening: EDTA removes Ca²⁺ and Mg²⁺ from hard water; (ii) medicine: EDTA is used to remove toxic metal ions (sometimes excess Ca²⁺) from the body.

book_ref.quote: When Group 2 salts dissolve in water, the metal ions become hydrated

blocks.prompt: 15 Seawater contains only a low concentration of Mg²⁺ ions. Trace how these ions end up as magnesium metal in the Dow process, explaining the purpose of each stage with its equation, and state why the process is regarded as so significant. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
The Dow process is a multi-step chemical and electrochemical process to extract Mg from the Mg²⁺ ions in seawater.

Stage 1, collecting Mg²⁺ as a solid: seawater is treated with calcium hydroxide (derived from limestone or oyster shells), which precipitates magnesium as insoluble magnesium hydroxide; the solid is filtered off.
Mg²⁺(aq) + Ca(OH)₂(s) → Mg(OH)₂(s) + Ca²⁺(aq)

Stage 2, converting to the chloride: Mg(OH)₂ is reacted with hydrochloric acid.
Mg(OH)₂(s) + 2HCl(aq) → MgCl₂(aq) + 2H₂O(l)
The MgCl₂ solution is concentrated and dried.

Stage 3, electrolysis: molten MgCl₂ is electrolysed in large electrolytic cells; pure magnesium forms at the cathode and chlorine gas at the anode.
Mg²⁺(l) + 2Cl⁻(l) → Mg(l) + Cl₂(g)

Significance: it extracts a valuable metal from an abundant, low-concentration source (seawater) on a massive industrial scale, and has revolutionized magnesium production.

book_ref.quote: is a multi-step chemical and electrochemical process

blocks.prompt: 16 Describe the production of quicklime from limestone in a lime kiln. Explain why carbon dioxide is removed continuously, and give the uses of quicklime. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Raw material: limestone, a naturally abundant sedimentary rock composed primarily of calcium carbonate. Making quicklime is one of the oldest and most fundamental industrial processes.

Process (calcination, a thermal decomposition): limestone is heated in a high-temperature furnace, the lime kiln (Figure 17.5), to typically 900-1000 °C. In modern kilns the ingredients are heated by circulating hot gases at the reaction temperature.
CaCO₃(s) → CaO(s) + CO₂(g)   (heat)

Removal of CO₂: the reaction is reversible in a closed container. CO₂ is removed continuously; this shifts the equilibrium to the right, giving faster production of a large amount of CaO.

Uses of quicklime (calcium oxide): construction (cement, mortar, plaster), agriculture (soil treatment), metallurgy (removing impurities in steel production), flue gas desulphurization, and various chemical industries.

book_ref.quote: This is one of the oldest and most fundamental industrial processes

blocks.prompt: 17 Describe the uses of Group 2 elements and their compounds in construction and in protecting the environment. Also give the uses of magnesium, strontium and beryllium mentioned in the chapter. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Construction:
• Calcium carbonate (limestone, marble, chalk): building material, cement, concrete, and filler in paper and plastics.
• Calcium oxide (quicklime) and calcium hydroxide (slaked lime): making cement, mortar and plaster; quicklime also removes impurities in steel production.
• Gypsum, CaSO₄·2H₂O: plasterboard (drywall) and plaster of Paris (CaSO₄·½H₂O).

Environment:
• CaO and CaCO₃ are used in flue gas desulphurization (wet scrubbing) to remove acidic SO₂ from power plant emissions, preventing acid rain.
• MgO is a refractory material (lining furnaces) due to its high melting point.

Metals:
• Magnesium: lightweight alloys (aerospace, automotive), fireworks and flares (bright burning).
• Strontium compounds: red colour in fireworks and flares.
• Beryllium: alloys for strength (springs, aerospace components) and X-ray tubes, as it is transparent to X-rays.

book_ref.quote: This is widely used as a building material, in cement, concrete

blocks.prompt: 18 Describe the medical uses of Group 2 compounds. Explain how the low solubility of Mg(OH)₂ and BaSO₄ makes them safe to use. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
• Magnesium hydroxide, Mg(OH)₂ (Milk of Magnesia): neutralizes excess stomach acid and is a mild laxative. Its low solubility makes it safe to use.
• Calcium carbonate: used in indigestion tablets as an antacid.
• Calcium compounds (calcium carbonate, calcium citrate): essential for strong bones and teeth; used as dietary calcium supplements to prevent osteoporosis.
• Magnesium compounds (magnesium sulphate, magnesium citrate): important for muscle and nerve function; treat magnesium deficiencies.
• Epsom salts, MgSO₄·7H₂O: laxative and used in baths.
• Barium sulphate, BaSO₄: barium meals for X-ray imaging of the digestive system. It is opaque to X-rays, and it is safe because it is highly insoluble and passes through the body without being absorbed (solubility 9.43 × 10⁻⁷ mol/100 g of water, Table 17.4).
• EDTA complexes: remove toxic metal ions from the body.

book_ref.quote: Calcium carbonate (CaCO₃) is also used in indigestion tablets as an antacid

blocks.prompt: 19 Group 2 compounds have diverse uses largely due to their basic nature and varying solubility. Explain this statement with examples from agriculture and other fields. (4 marks)
blocks.explanation:
Basic nature:
• Agriculture: CaCO₃ and Ca(OH)₂ are added to acidic soils to increase pH (neutralize acidity), making the soil more suitable for crop growth.
• Environment: CaO and CaCO₃ remove acidic SO₂ from power plant emissions (flue gas desulphurization), preventing acid rain.
• Medicine: Mg(OH)₂ and CaCO₃ neutralize excess stomach acid (antacids).

Varying solubility:
• Mg(OH)₂ is safe as Milk of Magnesia because of its low solubility.
• BaSO₄ is used in barium meals because it is highly insoluble and is not absorbed.
• Soluble compounds such as calcium nitrate and magnesium sulphate (Epsom salts) can be used as fertilizers.

Plant nutrients: calcium and magnesium are essential plant nutrients; calcium is crucial for cell wall development, and magnesium is the central atom in chlorophyll, vital for photosynthesis.

book_ref.quote: making the soil more suitable for crop growth
